note: Stand-in summaries of story version 3 (story-v3.json), written once from each scene's text by a model following the memory keeper's summary prompt (keeper/prompts.ts), for the offline recall measure. Invented story.

scenes.s1: By the end, Wren Hollis, apprentice to the dead surveyor Edric, has bolted the door of his house in Linmouth, packed his case with the finished maps of Carrow Fell, the field books and the seal, and settled on the floor beside it to wait out the night. Folded inside her jumper is Edric's letter, which tells her to take the survey to the Assize at Carrow by midsummer, register it in his name and hers before the Assize rises, and not to go by the coast road. A man called Gale, who says he acts for Warden Vey, knows her name and has promised to ask again in the morning. Wren had come home with a handcart to find the door open and Edric dead in his chair by the window, and she covered him with a blanket. On the table lay the maps, the ink barely dry, and the letter, which says the old levels on the north side of the fell run further than the Crown grant admits and that a dishonest survey would enrich Vey and ruin the town. Then Gale knocked, pleasant and clean in a good grey coat, and offered gold for the Carrow papers. She told him there were none and that Edric was dead. He studied her closely before he left, and she shut and bolted the door.
scenes.s2: By the end, Wren is standing in the garden of Edric's burning house with the survey case saved under her arm and her left arm burned from wrist to elbow, bandaged roughly with strips torn from one of Edric's spare shirts. Edric's body and the house are lost, and the men who broke in have run off along the shore road. She has decided not to go down into the town or take the coast road, where Gale would be watching, and to leave by the towpath up the river Linn instead. After midnight the front door was smashed in. Wren fled up the back stair to the loft with the case and hid behind chart tubes while the men searched the survey room and the chimney, found no seal, and guessed the girl had taken it. A flat-voiced man found her; she drove an elbow into his throat, and his lamp fell through the trap and set the paper-filled room alight, with Edric's blanketed body in it. She dragged the case clear of the burning skirting, her sleeve caught fire, and she escaped out the back. In the bean rows she peeled the melted jumper off the burn, cooled it in a water butt and bound it, and left as the roof fell in.
scenes.s3: By the end, Wren has crossed the Linn on Oskar Venn's ferry for her last two coppers and is walking up the far bank's track towards the salt road, which leads to Harrowgate, with half a lump of bread from Pell in her belly and a promise made: she will bring Pell, the ferryman's nine-year-old daughter, a blue glass bead from the Harrowgate market when she comes back this way. Oskar has guessed she is running from something and does not ask. He told her Carrow lies east and south, that she is on the wrong side of the water, and that it is a hundred miles round by the Harrowgate bridge and forty by the coast road. Wren had walked four miles overnight on the burned arm, half starved. At the landing she admitted the case was Master Edric of Linmouth's. On the punt she found Pell hidden under a tarpaulin. The girl asked what an apprentice does, looked at the red boundary pencil and the scorched strap, asked about the arm, and shared her bread. Wren told her Edric was dead.
scenes.s4: By the end, Wren has sold her grandfather's watch for five shillings, keeping its chain, bought a dun mare she named Thistle for four pounds, bought a halter and nosebag with the change, and is riding at the tail of Ash Penrose's herd of ninety cattle up the drove road towards Harrowgate. Ash, a rangy drover in a much-mended coat, helped her bargain and knows only that she is a surveyor bound for Harrowgate and then Carrow; he chose not to ask more. In return for a place by the drovers' fire she will count his cattle, which his man Tom cannot do. She had reached Fallow Cross after a day and a half on the salt road, sleeping in a shepherd's hut, her arm now smelling sweet under the bandage, which frightened her. At the horse fair she sold the watch, then Ash warned that the dun had a weak near hind but was the best she could afford, told her to keep her money in her fist, and talked the dealer down while she said four. They set out at first light with the herd, Tom singing, and Wren afraid of nothing behind her for the first time since the fire.
scenes.s5: By the end, Wren's burn has been washed, greased with Ash's goose grease and rebound in clean linen, and Ash has said he will redo it every day until it closes and that she must tell him at once if it smells sweet. He now knows she is a surveyor's apprentice, six years trained, bound for the Assize at Carrow to register a survey; she told him no more and he did not push. The party will reach Drake's Bottom in two days, where he recommended a barley broth, warned her off the meat, and said a smith will shoe Thistle for a shilling on his word. At noon Wren counted the herd at ninety, and Ash noticed she held her arm out from her side as if a wasp were on it. He made them stop at a spring, sat her on the trough and had her strip to the bandages. The burn ran from wrist to elbow, blistered and weeping, printed with the pattern of little flowers from the shirt cuff. Ash told of a burn he took at Drake's Bottom at twenty, remarked on how cool she was, and they went on.
scenes.s6: By the end, Wren has told Ash the whole truth, and he has promised to tell no one, ever, not Tom, not the boy, and not anyone at Drake's Bottom. She told him the case holds the seal and the last survey of her master, Edric Rone, of Carrow Fell, whose old silver levels run a mile and a half past the beck where Warden Vey's Crown grant says the mineral rights stop. Vey has been buying the freeholds round the fell for two years and, if the survey is not registered at the Assize in Edric's name and hers, can swear his own survey and take the fell. A man came to the door with gold, and men later burned the house. They had made eight miles by dusk and sheltered in a stone bothy while Tom and the boy held the cattle by the stream. Ash asked why men had burned the house; Wren weighed the lie against the truth and chose to trust him. He answered by telling of a fire at Drake's Bottom at twenty that he was blamed for, and how talk travels. He told her the smith there is called Reuben.
scenes.s7: By the end, Wren has crossed Haldon Bridge, having paid her rider's penny with her grandmother's brass compass, which is now in Mother Agate's coat pocket. She is left with a broken button and the brass watch chain and nothing else. Agate asked what was in the case and Wren would not answer. The herd and riders go on up the road beyond the bridge. In the afternoon of the fifth day the cattle reached the old three-arched bridge, where the elderly toll-woman Agate counted ninety-two head, including two strays, but took toll on ninety, a penny a beast and a penny the rider. Ash paid for the beasts, but Agate insisted the rider's penny was Wren's own to pay. Wren had spent four pounds on Thistle and five shillings at Drake's Bottom on shoeing, oats and a strip of leather for the nosebag, and had nothing left. She would not offer the case or the letter. She gave the compass, which her grandfather carried on the levels at Linmouth for forty years and her grandmother gave her at her apprenticeship, its needle trembling a quarter point east.
scenes.s8: By the end, Wren and Ash are riding on up through the beech wood towards open ground, wary that the attackers may return or wait ahead. Both men have fled, Wren still has the case with the letter inside it, her jumper has a torn hem, and Ash has a long knife cut from under his left eye down to the jaw, which she padded and bound with a strip of her jumper. Ash remarked that the men were not after the cattle and knew which of the ninety to come at. They had been riding under the new beech leaves, Ash talking about a bull that learned to open gates, when two men dropped from the bank. One seized Thistle's reins while the other pulled Wren off the saddle and tried to drag the case strap over her head; she held on, jarring the burned arm. Ash leapt in with his stick, took a skinning knife across the face, but bent the man's arm, dropped the knife and knocked him down. The first man ran and the second followed. Wren cleaned the wound with the nosebag, bound it, and fetched Thistle back.
scenes.s9: By the end, Thistle is left lame at Hobb's farm, where the farmer's wife will poultice her and keep her in a box for a fortnight or more at two shillings, which Wren promised to bring when she came back for her, giving her name and saying she was bound for Carrow. Wren rides on Cinder, a tall plain grey gelding with a white nose that Ash bought from the farmer and insists he is only lending. They had come out of the wood onto the moor, Ash's bandage white round his head. Two miles on, Thistle put her front foot in a rabbit hole and began to nod with lameness. Ash judged a deep bruise and said she could not carry Wren far, so they walked her half a mile down to the farm. The wife found a bruise with part of the hole driven into it, said weeks, not days, and that taking her out would lame her for good, and said she would not sell her. Wren unsaddled the mare, hung the tack on a peg, and said goodbye. Ash counted out coins for the grey, and they rode off.
scenes.s10: By the end, Wren has a small room under the roof of the Drover's Rest in Harrowgate, two shillings a week, paid out of money Ash refused to take back, and the innkeeper Sela Marr believes she is a wool buyer out of Linmouth with samples and books. Ash will go at first light with Tom to have the herd counted in at the cattle market and will come back for her at noon. Sela, warm, curious and a gossip, remarked that the Assize sits in three weeks and that wool men come for it. They had brought the herd in through the north gate after eight days on the road, put it in the pens, and taken the horses to the inn. Sela looked over the case, the bandage and the burned sleeve and questioned Wren, who said she burned her arm on a lamp. Ash said he had fallen on a gate, and Sela did not believe him. He warned Wren that Sela would have her name round the town by morning, and Wren said the wool story was the nearest true thing and would hold. Sela showed her up to the room, and she stood at the little window with her hand on the case, the town between her and Carrow.
scenes.s11: By the end, Wren knows that surveys are not registered at the assay office but must be laid in person before the Assize at Carrow, forty miles from Harrowgate, which sits at midsummer, the twenty-first, and rises when it is done. Today is the ninth, so she has nineteen days or must wait a year. The clerk plainly recognised the name Edric Rone, though he wrote nothing down, and was unkind to her. She woke in the inn with the burn healing and the cuff pattern still stamped in her skin, ate, asked Sela the way, and walked up through the market stalls. At the assay office she asked to register a survey; the clerk said the office only assays metal, keeps the town's weights and takes fees on cattle, and told her the surveyor or his sworn deputy must lay the instrument, field books and seal before the court. She asked how a dead man's survey could be entered in two names, and he said she must swear to it, that the court would not like it but would take it, and that she should be gone from Harrowgate. She turned back down the hill to find Ash at the inn by noon.
scenes.s12: By the end, Wren has sat up all night in her room at the Drover's Rest with the case on her knees and her clothes on, having heard Sela turn away a courteous stranger in a grey coat who came asking for a young woman from Linmouth with reddish hair and a brass-cornered surveyor's case. Sela insisted her guest was a wool buyer asleep in bed, and the man left, walking south towards the river. Ash has not come back, and seventeen days remain. Wren had spent the afternoon in the yard grooming Cinder and waiting for Ash, then ate in the taproom, where Sela asked nothing, and tended her burn by candlelight. When three soft, unhurried knocks came at the inn door below, she froze with the case in both hands and listened at the stairwell. Sela stalled and deflected, saying every traveller has a case and that she knew most of the town, and after a long silence the man said there was no one and wished her goodnight. Wren watched him from the window as he crossed the lamplight and vanished, then sat on the bed through the small hours.
scenes.s13: By the end, Wren has bought a single blue glass bead for a penny, to give Pell on the ferry as promised, and hidden it in the torn corner of her jumper pocket. Ash has sold ninety of the cattle for nineteen pounds eleven and six and kept the two strays, and the two of them sit on the cathedral steps eating pies, with eighteen days left. Wren has told Ash how she means to lay the survey and swear to it at the Assize. In the morning Sela fed her porridge and said Ash had come in at first light. Wren found him at the pens counting. She told him about the man at the door the night before, grey all over and with no mud on him; Ash guessed it was Gale and said not to talk about it in the street. They went through the market stalls to a pie man. On the way Wren looked at thread and knives and bread and bought nothing, then stopped at a glass-maker's stall and chose one blue bead, thinking of the girl on the punt, and told Ash she kept accounts.
scenes.s14: By the end, Bryn Tally, Ash's cousin, a broad carter and farrier from Harrowgate with an old burn scar across the back of one hand, has offered Ash and Wren two places under the canvas of her cart, going west the day after tomorrow with salt fish and dyed cloth for Fallow Cross and the villages under the fell. Wren, thinking of the forty miles, the seventeen days and the grey-coated man, asked which road west, and Bryn answered that they would be on it by noon. Ash's wound has healed to a pale pink scar. At the Drover's Rest, Sela told Wren a woman had waited an hour asking for Penrose. Bryn, whom Ash had sent for by word with a carter called Fenn, sized Wren up as the wool buyer and explained how she knew Ash. When Ash came in they embraced and joked about the scar and the gate. Bryn then said she was not asking, but she had noticed the surveyor's case between Wren's feet and the burned arm, that her brother had gone to Carrow, and that nobody looks under a carter's canvas.
scenes.s15: By the end, Wren has accepted Bryn's offer of two places on her cart: they will meet at the west gate of Harrowgate on the Fallow Cross road at first light in two days, on condition that the case never leaves Wren's hands. Bryn now knows, because Ash told her, that there is silver under Carrow Fell, that a survey of it is in the case, and that a man in town would pay to keep it off the record. She says she has no interest in silver and wants only to know who the man is; Wren refused to name him. Wren is furious that Ash broke his promise from the bothy. Bryn had asked why a wool buyer needed Carrow so badly, and Ash, who had already told her, let it come out. Wren stormed into the yard and Ash followed and admitted he had spent her secret to get the seat, said he would do it again, but promised to say nothing more to anyone. She went back in, and Bryn told Ash he had made his bed, pressed once for the name, and left.
scenes.s16: By the end, Wren has refused Gale's offer of twenty crowns in gold for the old man's papers and has worked out that he does not know what the papers are, which means he is only a messenger sent to fetch the case. Gale has told her he is in no hurry, that the offer stands, and that he knows the Assize sits at midsummer; he walked off towards the river. She went back in to Ash, shook her head once without speaking, and counted seventeen days. At dusk Wren went to the privy with the case under her arm. Returning, she met Gale at the mounting block, hat in hand, who named her Mistress Hollis and said Sela had called her a wool buyer, which he did not believe. He offered the crowns for whatever was in the case. She noticed he never mentioned the survey, the fell or the levels. He said he had been to the assay office, which stopped her briefly, and he added that careful men keep copies and that he would rather buy than take.
scenes.s17: By the end, Wren, Ash and Bryn are on the road west from Harrowgate, with seventeen days left, following Bryn's plan: go west to Fallow Cross, turn south at the fen, come back east to the Linn ferry below Linmouth and take the salt road south to Carrow. It is four days round rather than two, but Bryn is sure Gale will watch the one south road and its bridge, and Wren chose the ferry. Wren woke before dawn with her boots on and met Ash in the yard with the horses saddled. They went out through the stable arch to Bryn's loaded and sheeted cart and followed it up to the west gate, where Bryn paid the gatekeeper without mentioning the riders. On the road Ash objected that they were heading the wrong way for Carrow. Bryn explained that the road from the south gate is easy to watch. Wren recalled Gale saying there was time and understood he meant to let her run. They rode on through dry heat and dust.
scenes.s18: By the end, Bryn has paid Mother Agate six pence toll for the whole party at Haldon Bridge and they have crossed with sixteen days left. Agate wears Wren's grandmother's brass compass on a tarred cord outside her coat, laughed that it was the best toll she had had in ten years, and told Wren she would not get it back for sixpence or six pounds. Ash saw it and said nothing. They reached the bridge in the middle of the second morning, and Wren knew it from eight days earlier, when she had paid with the compass. Agate demanded toll on two riders, two horses and the loaded cart, and haggled Bryn from four pence to six. As the cart moved off Agate pulled the compass out on its cord, and Wren thought she would speak of the price. Instead the old woman laughed and said it was worth more than any sixpence. Wren kept her eyes on the far bank and counted the arches.
scenes.s19: By the end, Cinder has a new shoe fitted by Bryn at the roadside and the party is going on down the valley towards the fen, a day and a half away. Bryn will carry Wren because Ash comes with her, and Wren has told her the survey is her master's work, that there is silver under the fell and nothing on the record about it, and that a man in Harrowgate would pay to keep it that way. Bryn has a brother at Carrow, unseen for twelve years, so two of them have business there. Rain fell on the second day. When they stopped by a stand of thorn Wren found Cinder's off hind shoe gone. Bryn, who carries an anvil, hammer and tongs in the cart, lit a fire of thorn and reset the shoe, and charged Wren only a penny. While Ash slept on the bank, Bryn greased her whip and said she had not asked anything because she had worked it out from what she saw. Ash woke singing.
scenes.s20: By the end, Wren has left Thistle at Hobb's farm for another fortnight, two shillings to be paid when she comes back, on condition that the mare is not to be sold, lent or put to the cart. She has fourpence left, there are fourteen days to midsummer, and she rides on after the cart with Ash sitting behind her on Cinder. Bryn halted the cart at the turn to the farm and left the choice to Wren. In the paddock the mare stood with a poultice in sacking on her off fore, the heat gone from the coronet, and came to Wren's hand. The farmer's wife said she was not for riding yet; another week and the poultice would come off, then a week on grass. Wren spoke quietly to the mare, promised to come back, latched the gate, and rode on. Bryn asked whether she had the price in her head, and Wren said she did.
scenes.s21: By the end, Wren, Ash and Bryn have escaped across a ford at dusk after Gale and two riders stopped them. Bryn drove her cart straight down the bank at Gale and scattered the three men and horses in the water, and the party got up the far bank, with Gale standing in the ford in his ruined grey coat, watching Wren go. Gale now knows Wren's name and Bryn's. He greeted Wren from the shallows as Mistress Hollis, repeated his offer of twenty crowns, and admitted he does not know what is in the case and was only sent to fetch it, which Wren took as proof he had not been told. When he stepped forward and told Bryn to leave the girl and the case, Bryn said he was standing in the road and hit the horse. Wren put her heels to Cinder and followed at a trot through the water. Ash remarked that Gale would have her name across the county by Sunday, and she said he had it already.
scenes.s22: By the end, the three are camped three miles beyond the ford. Wren has refused Bryn's demand for a share of the claim, Bryn has dropped it, and they have agreed to cross the Linn at Oskar Venn's ferry below Linmouth and take the salt road south over the moor to Carrow, two days if the ground is wet. Thirteen days remain. Bryn said Gale knew too much and asked what the claim was worth, adding that she had carried Wren four days and taken Gale's name at a ford and wanted a share. Ash was furious and told her she was holding out her hand for a dead man's work. Wren answered that the survey was Edric's and had to be entered in his name and hers, that nothing in it could be shared, and that it would only stop being a lie. Bryn relented, asking only that the shoe be paid for, and warned that her name would be in it and she did not want her brother at Carrow hearing of her from a Warden's man. They ate, and left before first light.
scenes.s23: By the end, Wren has stood in the burned shell of Edric's house in Linmouth, found nothing in the gap behind the loose chimney brick where the seal tin was hidden, wept in front of Ash, and turned back up the lane with the case. Ash reminded her that Gale knows her name, the ferry is below the town, and thirteen days remain, and that Bryn will not drive the moor at night, so they must be on the hill before dark. They came over the moor in the afternoon and saw the coast and the black gap in the terrace. Bryn stayed on the cart. Wren walked down alone. The gables and chimney stood, the survey room had fallen in, and weeks of rain had streaked the soot. She found the scorched ring where Edric's chair had stood and a shape in the ash she did not touch. Ash came and stood near, she said she had sold her grandfather's watch, given up her compass and had fourpence, and he said it was still Edric's house.
scenes.s24: By the end, the three are sheltering from a storm in a turf-roofed shepherd's hut on the moor, with twelve days left. Wren is wearing a grey wool shirt found in a box under the bench, and she sits awake by the dying fire with Edric's map unrolled and resolved that she will get the survey to the Assize. Ash and Bryn sleep. The storm broke as they climbed from the coast, and Bryn lit a fire of kindling, turf and coal. Over supper Ash told how he left his father's few acres above Drake's Bottom at fifteen to drove cattle, lost two beasts in a snowdrift, and cried in a barn. Bryn said her father, a Harrowgate farrier, drank and made her the reason, and her hand scar was not from a forge; her brother went to Carrow twelve years ago, and she did not want the Warden's men carrying her name there first. Wren studied the map: the red Crown line, the black levels running a mile and a half past it, the word silver underlined, and what recording it would mean for Vey and the town.
scenes.s25: By the end, Wren, Ash and Bryn have come down to the swollen Linn. The ferry landing is under water and the punt lies hauled up on the far bank, but smoke from Oskar Venn's chimney shows he is at home. Wren has fourpence and means to ask him to take them across. Bryn says that if he refuses they will wait, and that if he never agrees they would go back and round by the south, at a cost of four days. The storm ended in the night. Wren had sat awake until the rain stopped, and found Bryn awake on the bench. Bryn predicted a flood and Ash called it a fine morning. They got Cinder and the cart down off the bank and followed the washed-out road down the valley, the ground running with water. Where the road gave a view they saw the river, wide and pale and carrying whole trees. Ash argued that a ferryman is there to cross water like this, and Bryn doubted it.
scenes.s26: By the end, all have crossed the flooded Linn on Oskar's punt, the cart first and the horses after in two trips, for Wren's double fare of fourpence, and are going up the track towards the salt road. Wren has given Pell the blue bead. Oskar first refused, saying he could not see his landing from the middle, but relented when Wren offered double; he remembered her as the girl with the burned arm who owed Pell a bead. Oskar and Bryn hauled on the cable, which went under the water. On the second trip Cinder balked and Ash bailed with his hat. Pell, who had been waiting on the bank, said Wren had come back, took the bead, and ran to the house. When Wren told her she would not be coming back this way, Pell said she would keep it and put it in her pocket. Oskar said the road was a slough past the second beck and told them of a stone barn at the top of the rise; he said it would rain Thursday, and Bryn said it would not.
scenes.s27: By the end, Wren sits alone by the dying fire in the common room of the Wheatsheaf in Carrow reading the last page of Edric's field book, where the signature block waits for two names. Two days remain before the Assize. They have two rooms, Bryn paying for the second, and Bryn has taken both horses to the smith and will not be back before morning. The landlord Rafe told them a man in a grey coat with no mud on him has asked at every door in Carrow since Monday about a survey, a case and anyone off the salt road. Wren thinks he does not know what it is; Ash thinks he knows and is only the hand. Ash said he would go to the Crown in the morning to hear a man with forty Galloway going north, and neither he nor Wren knew whether he would go. Wren said her next steps after registering were to collect Thistle at the farm and then walk the levels herself, including a drain above the second beck that Edric never checked.
scenes.s28: By the end, Wren and Ash have found the old adit on the north side of Carrow Fell, timbered and dripping, exactly where Edric's survey put it, and Wren says she wants to go down for something to eat and then lay the survey before the Assize. Ash had come back from the Crown with nothing, since the man with the Galloway had gone north on Tuesday, and he came up the fell with her as a witness. They climbed on foot, Ash leading Cinder, past old spoil heaps and pits full of black water, Wren identifying the wash and the leat. Fog came down over them. She pressed on counting her paces, lost the count, and said she felt the whole thing tilt. Ash told her to look at the ground, and she found a shallow groove: the leat from the pond to the adit, drawn to the chain on her survey. They followed it round the shoulder of the hill to a timbered black mouth under the crag. She held up the map against the hillside, and the drawing fitted the rock.
scenes.s29: By the end, the survey of Carrow Fell has been entered on the record of the Assize in the names of Edric Rone, sworn surveyor of Linmouth, deceased, and Wren Hollis, his apprentice. Wren swore that he made it and that she carried it, the instrument, field books and seal are filed with the roll, and Magistrate Ide told Gale the Warden may inspect the record and plead to it at the next Assize. Gale left with no expression on his face. Wren may buy a copy for two pence, and the Assize rises tomorrow. Ash waits at the foot of the lane with Cinder. Wren had come into town from the fell and was told by a clerk to return tomorrow, but after she named the survey he fetched the magistrate. She laid the case out in the chapter house, gave the substance aloud and offered to swear. Gale then came in with the Warden's warrant and asked to see the survey first; Ide refused him, took the survey into a side room with the clerk, and after a quarter of an hour returned with the entry made and its wax seal set.
scenes.s30: By the end, Wren and Ash are riding north out of Carrow at six, with the copy of the entry folded in her jumper over the letter, and Ash has said he will go with her to Haldon Bridge and then help her walk the levels of the fell, carrying the staff and counting paces, after the Fallow Cross fair; she is almost out of money and means to get Thistle from the farm for two shillings. Bryn has parted from them and driven south in her cart. Wren had bought the copy for two pence at the clerk's table. Bryn, in the square, said she was not stopping to be thanked, shook Wren's hand, told her the shoe was paid, and knocked her forehead against Ash's. Ash and Wren talked about whether he might have gone north with the Galloway; he said there is always another herd. Wren said she was twenty-two. She told him he needed a better coat, and he said it was dry, which was all he asked of a coat.

chapters.1: By the end of the chapter, Wren Hollis has fled Linmouth, crossed the Linn, bought a mare named Thistle at Fallow Cross and joined Ash Penrose's cattle drive up the drove road to Harrowgate, carrying her dead master's survey case with a burned left arm and almost no money. The chapter opens with Wren finding Edric dead in his chair and his letter telling her to take the Carrow Fell survey to the Assize, and Gale, who says he acts for Warden Vey, knocking to offer gold for the papers (scene 1). That night men break in and the lamp they drop burns the house with Edric in it; Wren escapes with the case and her arm burned, and takes the towpath (scene 2). At Oskar Venn's ferry she meets his daughter Pell and promises her a blue glass bead from Harrowgate, and Oskar points her toward the salt road (scene 3). At the Fallow Cross horse fair she sells her grandfather's watch, buys Thistle, and accepts a place with Ash's herd (scene 4).
chapters.2: By the end of the chapter, Wren is riding on from Hobb's farm on Cinder, a grey gelding that Ash has lent her, because Thistle is lame and has been left there. She has spent all her money and her grandmother's compass, and Ash, who has a knife cut down his cheek, knows the truth about the survey and has promised silence. Early in the chapter Ash dresses the burn with goose grease (scene 1). That night in a bothy Wren tells him everything about the silver levels, Warden Vey and the unregistered survey, and he promises to tell no one (scene 2). At Haldon Bridge she pays Mother Agate's toll with the compass (scene 3). In the beech wood two men ambush her for the case, and Ash is cut across the face driving them off (scene 4). Moving on across the moor, Thistle goes lame in a rabbit hole and is left at Hobb's farm to recover, and Ash lends Wren Cinder (scene 5).
chapters.3: By the end of the chapter, Wren is at the Drover's Rest in Harrowgate with about seventeen days to midsummer, and Bryn Tally, Ash's cousin, has offered her and Ash places on her cart going west, which Wren has not yet accepted. She has passed herself off as a wool buyer to the innkeeper Sela Marr, learned she has to reach Carrow, and bought Pell's bead. The herd arrives and Sela lodges her as a wool buyer (scene 1). At the assay office she learns surveys must be laid in person before the Carrow Assize, forty miles away, with nineteen days left (scene 2). A courteous man in a grey coat comes asking Sela for a girl with a surveyor's case, and Sela covers for her (scene 3). Ash sells the cattle, Wren tells him about the man, he guesses Gale, and she buys the blue bead (scene 4). Bryn appears and makes her offer (scene 5).
chapters.4: By the end of the chapter, Wren, Ash and Bryn have left Harrowgate by the west gate on a roundabout route and crossed Haldon Bridge again, where Mother Agate now wears Wren's compass on a cord, with sixteen days left. Bryn's route goes west, then south to the fen, then east to the Linn ferry and the salt road, because Gale would watch the south road. Ash told Bryn about the silver, so Wren is angry, but she accepts the cart on condition the case stays in her hands (scene 1). Gale then offers her twenty crowns for the old man's papers, she refuses and sees he doesn't know what they are (scene 2). They leave at dawn, Bryn explaining the longer way, and Wren chooses the ferry (scene 3). At Haldon Bridge Bryn pays the toll for all of them and Agate shows off the compass (scene 4).
chapters.5: By the end of the chapter, the three are camped beyond a ford where Gale tried to stop them, with thirteen days left. Gale now knows Wren's name, Bryn has been refused a share in the claim, and they have agreed to cross the Linn at Oskar's ferry and take the salt road to Carrow. In the rain Cinder casts a shoe and Bryn reshoes him at the roadside for a penny, and she and Wren talk (scene 1). They pass Hobb's farm, where Wren leaves Thistle for another fortnight at two shillings (scene 2). At dusk at a ford Gale and two riders confront them, and Bryn drives her cart at him and scatters them (scene 3). By the fire Bryn asks for a share of the claim, Wren refuses, and Bryn relents, worrying that her name could reach her brother (scene 4).
chapters.6: By the end of the chapter, the party have crossed the flooded Linn on Oskar's punt for Wren's last fourpence, and Pell has her blue bead. Twelve days remain, and they head up the track towards the salt road. Early on they reach Linmouth and Wren finds Edric's house a burned shell, with nothing in the hiding place, and weeps in front of Ash (scene 1). A storm drives them into a shepherd's hut, where Ash and Bryn tell of their pasts and Wren studies the map and resolves to reach Carrow (scene 2). The next morning they find the river in flood and the landing under water, with smoke from Oskar's chimney (scene 3). Oskar first refuses to cross, then agrees when Wren offers double, takes the cart and horses over in two trips, and Wren gives Pell the bead (scene 4).
chapters.7: By the end of the chapter, the survey of Carrow Fell is on the record in the names of Edric Rone and Wren Hollis, Gale has been turned away, Bryn has parted from them and driven south, and Wren and Ash are riding north out of Carrow. Ash has said he will come with her to Haldon Bridge and then help walk the levels, and she intends to collect Thistle for two shillings. At the Wheatsheaf, Rafe says a grey-coated man has asked after a survey since Monday, and Ash is unsure whether he will go north (scene 1). On the fell they find the old adit by following the leat in fog, exactly where Edric drew it (scene 2). At the Assize, Magistrate Ide considers the survey in private, Gale's demand to see it is refused, and the entry is made and the seal filed (scene 3). The next morning Bryn takes her leave and Ash says he will walk the levels with her (scene 4).
